title: A denarius was a day's pay
summary: Jesus' own parable prices a day in the vineyard at one denarius, and a soldier under Tiberius earned less than that. It is the yardstick for every other sum in the Gospels.
body: In the parable of the vineyard the landowner agrees with the labourers 'for a denarius a day' (Matthew 20:2) and pays every worker exactly that, so the story itself tells us the going day rate for hired agricultural work.

Independent evidence agrees. Tacitus records mutinous legionaries in AD 14 complaining that 'ten asses a day is the value set on life and limb' — ten asses is five-eighths of a denarius, so a farm hand in the parable was paid better per day than a Roman soldier (though the soldier was paid year-round).

The coin itself was a small silver piece about 19 mm across, roughly the size of a modern US penny or a 1-euro-cent coin, weighing about 3.9 g of nearly pure silver. The 'tribute penny' Jesus was handed in Matthew 22 was almost certainly one of these; the most common denarius in circulation in his lifetime carried Tiberius' head and the legend TI CAESAR DIVI AVG F AVGVSTVS — 'Tiberius Caesar, son of the divine Augustus'. That inscription is what makes 'whose image and inscription is this?' such a pointed question.

title: A year's wages poured out in one act
summary: The onlookers price the flask of nard at 'more than three hundred denarii'. At a denarius a day that is roughly a year of a labourer's income — and Pliny confirms the top perfumes really did cost that much.
body: Mark and John both put a number on the perfume: over 300 denarii (Mark 14:5; John 12:5). John adds the quantity — a litra, the Roman pound of about 327 g — and the grade, 'pure nard'.

Set beside Matthew 20:2 (one denarius = one day's work), 300 denarii is about 300 working days. How many days a labourer actually worked in a year is an estimate: a six-day week minus Sabbaths and the pilgrim festivals leaves roughly 300, which is why this is usually described as 'about a year's wages'. The figure is a comparison, not a conversion into modern money.

Pliny the Elder, writing a generation later, lists prices for luxury unguents that land in exactly this range: raw spikenard at 100 denarii per pound, and the costliest compounded perfume at 'from 35 to 300 denarii' per pound. He also notes that 'unguents keep best in alabaster boxes' — the very container Mark describes (see the Models tab for the flask).

Nard (Nardostachys jatamansi) grows in the Himalayas; every pound in Judea had crossed the Indian Ocean trade routes, which is where the price came from. Jesus' reply — 'she has done a beautiful thing' — lands harder once the sum is real: the value of a year of someone's labour, spent in a moment.

media.caption: Calcite ('alabaster') alabastron, Egypt, Ptolemaic period (305–31 BC). The long neck and narrow mouth kept perfume from evaporating; the neck was often snapped to open it, matching Mark's 'she broke the jar'.

title: Ten thousand talents: a debt bigger than the kingdom's tax income
summary: A talent was 6,000 denarii, so the first servant owed 60 million days' wages; Josephus says the whole of Herod's kingdom yielded about 900 talents a year. The second servant owed 100 denarii — about three months.
body: The parable deliberately stacks the two debts against each other. A talent was not a coin but a weight of silver reckoned at 6,000 drachmae/denarii, so 10,000 talents is 60,000,000 denarii. At one denarius a day, that is 60 million days of labour — on the order of 160,000 years for one worker (an estimate that assumes roughly 300 working days a year).

For scale, Josephus records the annual tax revenue of the territories Herod the Great left to his sons: 600 talents for Archelaus (Judea, Samaria, Idumea), 200 for Antipas (Galilee and Perea) and 100 for Philip — about 900 talents a year for the whole region. The servant's debt is more than eleven years of the entire kingdom's revenue. 'Ten thousand' (myrioi) was also the largest single number-word in Greek, so the hearer would take it as 'the biggest debt imaginable'.
The fellow servant's 100 denarii was real money — about three to four months' pay — which is the point: it is a genuine debt, dwarfed only by comparison.

title: The widow's two lepta
summary: Mark translates her gift for Roman readers: two lepta 'make a quadrans' — 1/64 of a denarius, about ten minutes of a labourer's day.
body: The lepton ('thin one') was the smallest bronze coin in circulation in Judea, the Jewish prutah. Most of those found in Jerusalem excavations were struck a century or more earlier under the Hasmonean king Alexander Jannaeus (103–76 BC) and were still in everyday use — worn, crude, and almost worthless individually.

Mark's aside, 'which make a kodrantēs' (Latin quadrans), fixes the value: a quadrans was a quarter of an as, and sixteen asses made a denarius, so her two coins were 1/64 of a day's wage. The arithmetic is exact; only the 'ten minutes' comparison is an estimate assuming a ten-hour working day.
Because Mark explains the coin in Roman terms, this verse is also one of the small internal clues that his Gospel was written with a non-Judean, probably Roman, audience in mind.

title: The two-drachma tax and the coin in the fish
summary: Every adult Jewish male owed a half-shekel a year to the temple (Exodus 30:13). It had to be paid in Tyrian silver, and a Tyrian shekel — a stater of four drachmae — paid for exactly two men.
body: The collectors ask whether Jesus pays 'the two-drachma tax'. That is the annual half-shekel of Exodus 30:13, reinterpreted after the exile as a standing temple levy (Nehemiah 10:32 has a third of a shekel; by the first century it was a half). The Mishnah (Shekalim 1:3) describes money-changers setting up tables in the provinces a month before Passover to collect it.

The Mishnah also specifies the coinage: temple dues were to be paid in 'Tyrian silver' (Bekhorot 8:7), because Tyre's shekels kept a reliably high silver content even though they bore the image of the god Melqart. A Tyrian shekel was a tetradrachm — four drachmae — so the single stater Peter finds in the fish (Matthew 17:27) covers two half-shekel payments: 'for me and for you'. The detail is precise, and it is why money-changing was necessary in the temple courts at all.
See the Models tab for the coin's proportions.

title: Thirty pieces of silver
summary: Thirty shekels is the Torah's compensation for a slave killed by an ox. Matthew names no coin, so any modern value is an estimate — if they were Tyrian shekels it was about four months' wages.
body: Matthew is the only Gospel to give the price, and he gives it in a form that echoes two Old Testament texts: Exodus 21:32, where thirty shekels is what an owner receives for a slave gored to death, and Zechariah 11:12–13, where the prophet is paid 'thirty pieces of silver' as a contemptuous wage and throws it into the temple treasury.

The coin type is not stated. If the priests paid in the temple's own currency, Tyrian shekels (see the temple-tax card), thirty of them would be 120 denarii — roughly four months of a labourer's pay. That conversion is an inference, not a datum; what the text itself supplies is the allusion: the price of a slave.

title: Two denarii at the inn
summary: The Samaritan leaves two days' wages with the innkeeper and promises to cover any overrun — an open-ended guarantee, not a tip.
body: Two denarii is two days of a labourer's pay (Matthew 20:2). How many nights that bought is an estimate: comparisons with Roman price evidence suggest lodging and basic food ran a fraction of a denarius a day, so two denarii plausibly covered a week or more of care. The decisive detail is the promise that follows — 'whatever more you spend, I will repay you' — which turns a stranger's act into a standing liability for a man he will never see again.

title: Twenty shekels for Joseph — and why the number keeps rising
summary: Joseph is sold for twenty shekels of silver, Exodus fixes the compensation for a gored slave at thirty, and Assyrian records of a few centuries later run to fifty or sixty. Each figure sits where the documented market price sat at that time.
body: Genesis 37:28 prices Joseph at twenty shekels of silver. Exodus 21:32 sets thirty shekels as what an ox's owner pays when the animal gores someone else's slave. Leviticus 27:3-7 scales vow-valuations from three to fifty shekels by age and sex. Zechariah 11:12-13 has a shepherd paid off with thirty pieces of silver and calls it a contemptible sum.

Cuneiform sale contracts give an independent price curve. In the Third Dynasty of Ur, around 2100-2000 BC, ten shekels is the commonest price for a slave. Through the first half of the second millennium — roughly 1800-1700 BC, the Old Babylonian period — twenty shekels is the standard figure, and Hammurabi's laws assume it. Texts from Nuzi and Ugarit in the later second millennium sit around thirty. By about 1000 BC Assyrian documents are recording fifty to sixty shekels for a male slave, and Persian-period prices are higher still.

So the biblical figures are not a flat set of round numbers: twenty, thirty and the Leviticus scale each land near the going rate for the era each text is set in. Kenneth Kitchen pressed this as an argument that the traditions preserve authentic period detail rather than being composed wholesale at a much later date.

Two cautions, because the argument is often overstated. The correlation shows that the figures are plausible for those periods; it cannot by itself date the writing of the texts, since a later author could use traditional numbers. And prices varied by region, by the health and skill of the person sold, and by whether the sale was distressed — the 'standard' figures are averages across scattered contracts, so this card is marked as consensus rather than evidence.

title: Why there were money changers in the temple at all
summary: The annual half-shekel had to be paid in Tyrian silver — the purest coin in circulation, and one stamped with a pagan god. Every pilgrim arriving with Roman or provincial money therefore had to change it first, which is what the tables were for.
body: Exodus 30:13-15 requires every man counted in Israel to give half a shekel 'according to the shekel of the sanctuary'. By the Second Temple period this was an annual levy, collected before Passover, and the Mishnah rules that the sanctuary dues are reckoned 'in Tyrian coinage' (Bekhorot 8:7).

The reason was metallurgical. From about 126 BC the mint of Tyre struck shekels and half-shekels of unusually pure silver — assays put them at roughly 94-97% — and held that standard for well over a century, while Roman provincial silver was debased. For a fixed weight-based temple due, a coin whose silver content could be relied on was worth insisting on.

The irony was not lost on anyone. The Tyrian shekel carries the head of Melqart-Heracles on the obverse and an eagle on the reverse, with the legend 'of Tyre the holy and inviolable'. The purest coin available for the temple of the God of Israel was a coin bearing a Phoenician god.

So the moneychangers were performing a necessary service: pilgrims arriving with denarii, drachmas or local bronze could not pay the levy directly. The Gospels' complaint is not that the exchange existed but what it had become — 'you have made it a den of robbers' (Mark 11:17, quoting Jeremiah 7:11), a charge about the commission taken and the place it was taken in rather than about currency conversion as such.
The same coinage stands behind Matthew 17:24-27, where the two-drachma tax for two men is settled with a single stater — a Tyrian shekel being worth four drachmas.

title: The lost coin, and why she lit a lamp to find it
summary: A drachma was about a day's wage, so one of ten was ten per cent of a small household's reserve. Sweeping a windowless single-room house by lamplight for it was a rational response, not an extravagant one.
body: The Greek drachma was roughly equivalent in value to the Roman denarius, and Jesus prices a day's labour at a denarius elsewhere (Matthew 20:2). Ten drachmas is therefore something like a fortnight's earnings for a labourer — and for the woman in the parable, evidently the whole of what she has.

The lamp and the broom are the realistic part. A village house of the period was typically one room with a beaten-earth or rough stone floor and one small high window or none; even at midday the corners were dark. A small silver coin lost in that floor would not be found by looking. So she lights a lamp — an expense in itself, since lamp oil cost money — sweeps the floor to hear it move, and searches carefully until she finds it.

There is a further suggestion often made about the ten coins: that they were a woman's marriage headdress or dowry ornament, strung as a set, so that losing one spoiled the whole. This is possible and is attested in later Near Eastern custom, but Luke says nothing of it and no first-century evidence establishes it for Galilee. It is noted here as a suggestion, not a fact.

The parable's force needs neither embellishment. The sum is small to a rich hearer and serious to a poor one, and the point of the pairing with the lost sheep is that the search is proportionate to what the searcher can afford to lose — which in the third parable of the chapter turns out to be a son.
